C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards in developed economies when adjusted for rising income inequality
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies when adjusted for rising income inequality]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Income Distribution Database (IDD) and National Accounts data for GDP per capita trends (2000-2023) — Directly test the hypothesis by comparing GDP per capita growth with median income growth and income share of the top 10% across OECD countries over the post-2000 period. If GDP per capita rises while median income stagnates or falls, this supports the claim that GDP per capita underestimates declines in material living standards for the majority.

[PATH:literature] Piketty, Saez, and Zucman (2018) 'Distributional National Accounts' (DINA) methodology and updated series for the US and other OECD economies — Provides a rigorous theoretical and empirical framework for adjusting national income for distributional changes. Reviewing their results for post-2000 trends in real income growth for bottom 90% versus top 10% can confirm or refute the extent to which GDP per capita masks declining living standards for most households.

[PATH:empirical] LIS Cross-National Data Center (Luxembourg Income Study) microdata on household disposable income and consumption inequality — Allows for constructing alternative measures of material well-being (e.g., median equivalized disposable income, consumption floors) across OECD countries. Comparing these to GDP per capita trends would directly test whether the standard metric systematically overstates improvements in living standards when inequality rises.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
C006.object: material living standards in developed economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards in developed economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index, annual reports and microdata (e.g., housing, income, jobs, work-life balance, health, education, environment, social connections, civic engagement, and life satisfaction) — Directly compares GDP per capita with multidimensional well-being indicators across OECD countries post-2000, allowing empirical test of whether GDP per capita diverges from material living standards when non-market goods, inequality, and public services are considered.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of the 'Beyond GDP' literature, including Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission (2009) and subsequent updates (e.g., OECD's 'How's Life?' series), and critiques such as those by Deaton (2013) or Fleurbaey (2009) — Provides theoretical and empirical arguments both supporting and challenging the inadequacy claim, synthesizing evidence on measurement biases, distributional issues, and the role of non-monetary factors in material living standards.

[PATH:empirical] Cross-country panel data on household consumption, wealth, and subjective well-being (e.g., Luxembourg Income Study, World Bank's Global Consumption Database, Gallup World Poll) matched with national accounts GDP per capita — Enables direct regression or discrepancy analysis to test whether GDP per capita systematically misrepresents material conditions (e.g., consumption, asset poverty, or life satisfaction) in developed economies, controlling for time and country fixed effects.

C007.subject: GDP growth in post-industrial economies
C007.object: aggregate subjective life satisfaction when environmental degradation exceeds a regenerative threshold
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth in post-industrial economies aggregate subjective life satisfaction when environmental degradation exceeds a regenerative threshold]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) linked to national environmental degradation indicators (e.g., ecological footprint, air quality indices) for post-industrial economies from 2000 onward — Directly tests the correlation between GDP growth and subjective life satisfaction while controlling for environmental degradation levels relative to a regenerative threshold, using panel data over time and across countries specified in the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Empirical studies on the 'Easterlin Paradox' and the 'threshold hypothesis' in environmental psychology and ecological economics, particularly those examining the moderating role of environmental quality on the GDP-wellbeing relationship — Reviews existing evidence on whether the GDP-satisfaction link weakens or reverses under high environmental stress, providing theoretical grounding and empirical benchmarks for the proposed threshold effect.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational models integrating macroeconomic growth dynamics with ecological feedbacks and agent-based subjective wellbeing functions, calibrated to post-industrial economies — Allows simulation of the hypothesized negative correlation under varying environmental degradation scenarios, testing causal mechanisms and the existence of a regenerative threshold beyond which wellbeing declines despite GDP growth.

qualifier.temporal: post-2000, during periods of sustained environmental stress
qualifier.geographic: post-industrial economies in North America, Western Europe, and East Asia

C008.subject: GDP growth
C008.object: improved life satisfaction and incentivized environmental policies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth improved life satisfaction and incentivized environmental policies]

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report (annual data for OECD countries, 1990-2020) combined with GDP per capita growth rates from OECD Statistics — Directly tests the correlation between GDP growth and life satisfaction over the specified temporal and geographic scope, allowing for panel data analysis to confirm or refute the relationship.

[PATH:empirical] Environmental Policy Stringency Index (OECD) and GDP growth data, analyzed via Granger causality tests — Assesses whether GDP growth incentivizes stricter environmental policies or vice versa, addressing the causal direction implied in the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on the Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) and subjective well-being in OECD countries — Synthesizes existing evidence on the trade-offs and synergies between GDP growth, environmental quality, and life satisfaction, providing theoretical grounding and identifying gaps in the disputed claim.

C011.subject: GDP adjusted for inequality and non-market factors
C011.object: subjective life satisfaction than unadjusted GDP in post-industrial economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP adjusted for inequality and non-market factors subjective life satisfaction than unadjusted GDP in post-industrial economies]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and Gallup World Poll microdata (2000-2020) — compare subjective well-being scores with GDP per capita versus the OECD's 'GDP per capita adjusted for income inequality' and 'Household adjusted disposable income' series. — Directly tests the hypothesis by regressing life satisfaction on both unadjusted and adjusted GDP measures in post-industrial economies, controlling for non-market factors like unpaid work and environmental quality.

[PATH:literature] Systematic literature review and meta-analysis of studies using the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) or Inclusive Wealth Index (IWI) vs. GDP to predict life satisfaction in high-income countries. — Synthesizes existing empirical findings across multiple post-industrial contexts to assess whether adjusted metrics consistently outperform GDP in explaining subjective well-being variance.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework: 'Easterlin Paradox' and 'Capabilities Approach' (Sen, 1985; Kahneman & Deaton, 2010) — model why non-market factors (e.g., leisure, health, social trust) and inequality should moderate the GDP-life satisfaction link. — Provides causal reasoning for why adjusted GDP may be a stronger predictor, allowing derivation of testable predictions about the relative importance of distribution and non-market goods in post-industrial contexts.
